nature-clim-281.title: Microgrids: small power systems that can go it alone
nature-clim-281.text: A microgrid is a small power system with an escape hatch. It groups generation, storage and loads, and normally runs connected to the main grid. It can also disconnect and operate autonomously, much like the {{ref:nature-clim-280}} it often draws on. The link to the macrogrid is a single point of common coupling, and that is the point that can be disconnected. Inside, generation and loads are usually interconnected at low voltage and can run on DC, AC or both.

nature-clim-284.title: Biomass: energy and carbon stored in living matter
nature-clim-284.text:
Biomass is material produced by the growth of microorganisms, plants or animals. The main types are woody, herbaceous and agricultural, aquatic, animal-derived, microbial and waste-derived. It is a renewable energy source and a chemical feedstock, though its energy content is low relative to coal and petroleum and its oxygen content high.

The crops matter. First-generation biofuels and bioplastics come from energy-dense crops such as rapeseed, sugarcane or corn, and they raise crop prices and take arable land from food. Second-generation biomass, such as wood chippings, grass or solid waste, is far harder to convert because of its varied mixture of compounds. Research continues because it can reuse waste.

Ecologists use the word differently, for the total mass of organisms in an ecosystem, usually expressed as carbon. A 2017 estimate for the whole biosphere is about 550 Gt C, with about 450 Gt C of it in terrestrial plants. Remote sensing such as NDVI is commonly used to estimate biomass over large areas.

nature-clim-286.title: Weathering: how rock slowly becomes soil
nature-clim-286.text:
Rock does not stay rock. Water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living organisms wear down rocks, soils and minerals, and the process is called weathering. It happens in place, which separates it from erosion, where water, ice, wind and gravity carry rock and minerals away.

The processes are physical or chemical. Water is the principal agent of both, with oxygen, carbon dioxide and organisms also important. Granite shows the result: its minerals convert to clay minerals and iron oxides, and the soil left behind is depleted in calcium and sodium and enriched in aluminium and potassium.

The pace can be very slow. Basaltic ocean crust loses about 15% of its density per 100 million years. Human works weather too. Buildings, statues, wood, paint and plastics all decay, faster under acid rain or ultraviolet light. Two kinds of process do the work, and the entries that follow take each in turn.

nature-clim-285.title: Pyrolysis: heating biomass without oxygen
nature-clim-285.text:
Pyrolysis cooks organic matter in a sealed, oxygen-free space until its covalent bonds break. It yields char, a carbon-rich solid, along with condensable liquids such as oils and tar, and non-condensable gases. Unlike combustion or hydrolysis it adds no oxygen or water. It is the basis of several ways to make fuel from lignocellulosic {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, such as switchgrass, sawdust, straw, rice hulls and manure.

Methane pyrolysis gives hydrogen and solid carbon in one step, with no deep injection of carbon dioxide needed. Used on municipal solid and plastic waste it mainly cuts volume; recovering monomers is neither clean nor economically competitive in practice. The risks are explosion if oxygen is present and toxic gases such as carbon monoxide, greatest at start-up, shut-down and upsets.

nature-clim-287.title: Chemical weathering: rock rewritten by reaction
nature-clim-287.text:
In chemical weathering, water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change what it is made of. Primary minerals become secondary minerals, other substances leave as solutes, and the most stable minerals remain. The rock moves toward equilibrium with surface conditions. The main reactions are dissolution, hydrolysis (often acid hydrolysis, turning minerals into clay), oxidation of Fe2+ to iron oxides, and hydration.

Life speeds all this up. Albite and muscovite weather twice as fast in live soil, and lichen-covered granite weathered 3x to 4x faster than bare rock. Plants and microbes act by releasing chelating compounds, carbon dioxide and organic acids.

nature-clim-288.title: Physical weathering: breaking rock without changing it
nature-clim-288.text: Physical weathering, also called mechanical weathering, breaks rock into smaller fragments without chemical change. Its types include freeze-thaw, thermal stress, pressure release (unloading) and salt-crystal growth. Water expands in volume by 9.2% on freezing, yet ice segregation is now thought a more important frost mechanism than frost wedging. It is usually much less important than chemical weathering, but it can matter in subarctic or alpine settings.

nature-clim-274.title: Ozone depletion: the thinning of the shield above us
nature-clim-274.text:
In 1974 Frank Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina suggested that long-lived organic halogen compounds such as CFCs could deplete ozone. Ozone depletion is now defined as a lowered total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere, plus a much larger springtime decrease over the polar regions, observed since the late 1970s.

The main causes are manufactured halocarbons used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants and foam-blowing agents, called ozone-depleting substances. The ozone layer absorbs UVB light, so depletion raises surface UVB, which could increase skin cancer. That was the reason for the Montreal Protocol.

The treaties came early. The Vienna and Montreal conventions were put in place before a scientific consensus existed or key uncertainties were resolved. They seem to have worked: since the Protocol was adopted and strengthened, concentrations of the most significant CFCs have declined. Effective equivalent chlorine peaked in 1994 and had dropped about 10 percent by 2008.

nature-clim-275.title: The Antarctic ozone hole
nature-clim-275.text: In May 1985 British Antarctic Survey scientists reported in Nature that ozone over Antarctica was falling, and the decline was far larger than anticipated. The ozone hole is the area of the Antarctic stratosphere where ozone has dropped to as low as 33 percent of pre-1975 values. It appears in the Antarctic spring, September to early December, when strong westerly winds form a polar vortex in which over 50 percent of lower stratospheric ozone is destroyed. It is measured as reduced total column ozone in Dobson units, and actual hole values are in the 150-100 DU range.

nature-clim-276.title: Ozone-depleting substances: the chemicals behind the hole
nature-clim-276.text:
Ozone-depleting substances are halogenated chemicals, chiefly CFCs, that are mainly responsible for man-made ozone depletion. The total effective chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere is expressed as equivalent effective stratospheric chlorine, or EESC.

CFCs are well mixed globally. Their weight does not keep them from the stratosphere, because wind mixes atmospheric gases. Some substances escape the ban. Very short-lived ones, which degrade in under 6 months, are allowed by the Montreal Protocol. Of these, 90% are natural and 10% manmade, such as dichloromethane.

nature-clim-277.title: The Global Environment Facility: a fund for global goods
nature-clim-277.text:
The Global Environment Facility is the largest multilateral funder of biodiversity, distributing over $1 billion a year on average. It gives grants and blended finance to developing countries for biodiversity, climate change, international waters, land degradation, pollutants and forests. In all it has provided more than $22 billion in grants and mobilized $120 billion in co-financing for over 5,200 projects.

It began in October 1991 as a $1 billion World Bank pilot and became a permanent separate institution at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. The World Bank has been trustee since 1994. It is the financial mechanism for the CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD, Stockholm Convention and Minamata Convention, and it supports the Montreal Protocol. Donors pledged a record $5.33 billion in June 2022 for the replenishment cycle running to June 2026. Its Small Grants Programme supported nearly 27,000 civil society and community initiatives in 136 countries.

nature-clim-279.title: How the GEF is governed
nature-clim-279.text: The GEF is governed through an Assembly, a Council, a Secretariat, agencies, a scientific panel and an Independent Evaluation Office. The Assembly of all 184 member countries meets every three to four years at ministerial level. The Council is the main governing body. It has 32 members (14 developed, 16 developing, 2 transition economies), meets twice annually and decides by consensus. The Independent Evaluation Office reports directly to the Council and evaluates the Facility's impact and effectiveness.

nature-clim-278.title: The incremental cost principle: paying only for the global extra
nature-clim-278.text: The GEF does not pay for a whole project. It funds the incremental, or additional, costs of turning a project with national benefits into one with global environmental benefits. It provides new and additional grants and concessional funding to cover those costs.
